summary: Introduces the set of DNS Security Extensions in one place and points to the main RFCs that define them. It states that using DNSSEC for origin authentication of DNS data is the best current practice. It does not update the earlier DNSSEC documents.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC is the set of standards that let a resolver check that a DNS answer really came from the zone it claims to. This RFC gathers the documents that define it in one place and records the IETF's view that using it is the right thing to do.

subtitle: One document that gathers the DNSSEC standards and says to use them.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC is spread across three core documents and dozens of extensions, and someone deploying it needs to know which ones matter.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the core documents, the omnibus update that became part of the core, the algorithm documents, and the main extensions, and points at the IANA registries that relate to DNSSEC.
tldr.outcome: It states plainly that using DNSSEC for origin authentication of DNS data is the best current practice, and gives one reference for other specifications that want to refer to DNSSEC.

today: RFC 9364 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 237) and has not been obsoleted or updated. It does not update any of the RFCs it lists, so the core DNSSEC documents still define the protocol.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
The core specification for what we know as DNSSEC, the combination of RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, describes a set of protocols that provide origin authentication of DNS data. RFC 6840 updates and extends those core documents without fundamentally changing the way DNSSEC works.

This document lists the RFCs that should be considered by someone creating an implementation of, or deploying, DNSSEC as it is currently standardized. Although an effort was made to be thorough, the reader should not assume the list is comprehensive. It uses the terminology of those documents without defining that terminology, and it points to the relevant IANA registry groups that relate to DNSSEC. It does not point to standards that rely on zones needing to be signed by DNSSEC, such as DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a reading list with a verdict attached, not a new protocol. It says which documents matter and that the whole thing should be used.

sections.title: DNSSEC as a Best Current Practice
sections.content:
Using the DNSSEC set of protocols is the best current practice for adding origin authentication to DNS data. To date, no Standards Track RFCs offer any other method for such origin authentication of data in the DNS.

More than 15 years after the DNSSEC specification was published, it is still not widely deployed. Recent estimates are that fewer than 10% of the domain names used for websites are signed, and only around a third of queries to recursive resolvers are validated. This low level of deployment does not affect whether using DNSSEC is a best current practice; it indicates that the value of deploying it is often considered lower than the cost.

Nonetheless, the significant deployment of DNSSEC beneath some top-level domains and the near-universal deployment of DNSSEC for the top-level domains in the DNS root zone demonstrate that DNSSEC is applicable for implementation by both ordinary and highly sophisticated domain owners.
sections.plainLanguage: It is not used much yet, and the RFC says that is a cost calculation rather than a reason to think it is a bad idea. Signing the root zone shows it works at the largest scale there is.

sections.title: The Core Documents
sections.content:
What is called DNSSEC is the third iteration of the specification. RFC 2065 was the first and RFC 2535 the second, and the earlier iterations have not been deployed on any significant scale.

The three current core documents cover different topics. RFC 4033 is an overview of DNSSEC, including how it might change the resolution of DNS queries. RFC 4034 specifies the DNS resource records used in DNSSEC, and obsoletes many RFCs about earlier versions. RFC 4035 covers the modifications to the DNS protocol incurred by DNSSEC, including signing zones, serving signed zones, resolving in light of DNSSEC, and authenticating DNSSEC-signed data.

At the time the core documents were published, someone could build a DNSSEC implementation of signing software, of a DNSSEC-aware authoritative server, or of a DNSSEC-aware recursive resolver from those three documents plus a few older RFCs specifying the cryptography. RFC 2536 defines how to use the DSA signature algorithm, and DSA was thinly implemented and can safely be ignored. RFC 3110 defines how to use the RSA signature algorithm, and RSA is still among the most popular signing algorithms for DNSSEC.

Later RFCs update the core documents. RFC 6840 is an omnibus update that has itself become a core document: besides covering new requirements from new DNSSEC RFCs, it describes important security and interoperability issues that arose during deployment of the initial specifications, particularly after the DNS root was signed in 2010, and it lists some errors in the examples of the core specifications. It brings a few additions into the core, making NSEC3 as much a part of DNSSEC as NSEC, and making the SHA-256 and SHA-512 hash functions part of the core. RFC 9077 changes how TTL values are calculated in DNSSEC processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Three documents cover the ideas, the records and the protocol changes. Later documents patch them, and one of those patches is now treated as core itself.

sections.title: Algorithms and Their Age
sections.content:
Cryptographic algorithms typically weaken over time as computing power improves and new analysis emerges. Two new signing algorithms have been adopted by the DNSSEC community: the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm and the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm. Both have become very popular signing algorithms in recent years. The GOST signing algorithm was also adopted but has seen very limited use, likely because it is a national algorithm specific to a very small number of countries.

Implementation developers who want to know which algorithms to implement in DNSSEC software should refer to RFC 8624. That specification is only about what algorithms should and should not be included in implementations; it is not advice about which algorithms zone operators should use for signing, nor which recursive resolver operators should use for validation.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing algorithms age, so newer ones were added. Implementers should look at a separate document that says which to build in and which to leave out.

sections.title: Extensions to DNSSEC
sections.content:
The DNSSEC community has extended the core and the cryptographic algorithms, both in describing good operational practice and in new protocols. The RFC lists several of them.

RFC 5011 describes a method to help resolvers update their DNSSEC trust anchors in an automated fashion, and this method was used in 2018 to update the DNS root trust anchor. RFC 6781 is a compendium of operational practices that may not be obvious from reading just the core specifications. RFC 7344 describes using the CDS and CDNSKEY resource records to help automate the maintenance of DS records in the parents of signed zones, and RFC 8078 extends it by showing how to do initial setup of trusted relationships between signed parent and child zones.

RFC 8198 describes how a validating resolver can emit fewer queries in signed zones that use NSEC and NSEC3 for negative caching, and RFC 9077 updates it with respect to the TTL fields in signed records.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions cover the everyday work: keeping the trust anchors fresh, handing a signed zone over to its parent, and answering negative questions without asking as often.

sections.title: Other Documents of Interest
sections.content:
A further list of documents may be of value to someone implementing or operating DNSSEC.

RFC 4470 describes how to construct DNSSEC NSEC resource records that cover a smaller range of names than called for by RFC 4034; by generating and signing these records on demand, authoritative name servers can effectively stop the disclosure of zone contents otherwise made possible by walking the chain of NSEC records in a signed zone. RFC 6975 specifies a way for validating end-system resolvers to signal to a server which digital signature and hash algorithms they support.

RFC 7129 provides additional background commentary and some context for the NSEC and NSEC3 mechanisms used by DNSSEC to provide authenticated denial-of-existence responses, which is particularly important for understanding their use. RFC 7583 describes the issues surrounding the timing of events in the rolling of a key in a DNSSEC-secured zone, and RFC 7646 defines Negative Trust Anchors, which can be used to mitigate DNSSEC validation failures by disabling DNSSEC validation at specified domains.

RFC 7958 describes the format and publication mechanisms IANA has used to distribute the DNSSEC trust anchors. RFC 8027 describes problems that a validating resolver, stub resolver or application might run into within a non-compliant infrastructure. RFC 8145 specifies two different ways for validating resolvers to signal to a server which keys are referenced in their chain of trust. RFC 8499 contains lists of terminology used when talking about DNS, with Sections 10 and 11 covering DNSSEC, and RFC 8509 specifies a mechanism that will allow an end user and third parties to determine the trusted key state for the root key of the resolvers that handle that user's DNS queries. RFC 8901 presents deployment models for the scenario where each DNS provider independently signs zone data with their own keys and describes the key-management requirements. RFC 9276 provides guidance on setting NSEC3 parameters based on recent operational deployment experience.
sections.plainLanguage: A longer reading list for the details that bite in practice: hiding zone contents, timing of key changes, what to do when validation fails, and how to measure the trust state of a resolver.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA already has three registry groups that relate to DNSSEC: DNSSEC algorithm numbers, DNSSEC NSEC3 parameters, and DNSSEC DS RRtype digest algorithms.

The rules for the DNSSEC algorithm registry were set in the core RFCs and updated by RFC 6014, RFC 6725 and RFC 9157. This document does not update or create any registry groups or registries.
sections.plainLanguage: Three lists of assigned numbers govern the cryptography and the denial-of-existence parameters, and this RFC leaves them alone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: All of the security considerations from all of the RFCs referenced in this document apply here.
sections.plainLanguage: The security guidance is the guidance of the documents it points to, unchanged.
